questions.question: How do you implement JWT authentication from scratch in Spring Security?
questions.title: How to Implement JWT Authentication from Scratch in Spring Security
questions.direct_answer: JWT auth in Spring Security needs three things: a **`OncePerRequestFilter`** that extracts and validates the JWT from `Authorization: Bearer ...`, a **token util** for generation/validation, and a **`SecurityFilterChain`** with **`SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS`**, **CSRF disabled**, and the filter registered **before `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`**. The signed token lets the server verify authenticity without a per-request DB hit. **For most apps that only validate tokens** (not issue them), use Spring's **OAuth2 Resource Server** (`spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server`) instead — zero custom filter code, JWKS rotation, and standardized claims handling.

interviewer_intent.testing: Hands-on knowledge of stateless authentication — can the candidate wire up a complete JWT flow without scaffolding?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Storing JWTs in localStorage without understanding XSS risk, or forgetting to set SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS, causing sessions to be created unnecessarily.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss token expiry, refresh token strategy, signing algorithms (HS256 vs RS256), and token revocation challenges.

sections.title: Custom JWT Auth Has Four Easy-to-Miss Pieces
sections.content:
Implementing JWT authentication in Spring Security is mechanically straightforward — generate a token at login, validate it on every request.
- **The security mistakes are where real apps break.** Storing tokens in `localStorage` exposes them to XSS.
- Forgetting `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS` means Spring creates sessions alongside JWT, wasting memory.
- Using a weak HS256 secret makes tokens forgeable.

Before writing custom code, consider Spring Security 6's **OAuth2 Resource Server** (`spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server`). For apps that **validate** tokens (not issue them), it requires zero custom filter — just configuration. The custom path is for apps that ARE the issuer (not delegating to Keycloak/Auth0/Okta).

**Custom implementation has four components:**
- **`JwtUtil`** — token generation and validation (wraps `jjwt` or `nimbus-jose-jwt`)
- **`OncePerRequestFilter`** subclass — extracts and validates token per request
- **Login endpoint** — calls `AuthenticationManager`, generates token on success, returns it
- **`SecurityFilterChain`** — `STATELESS`, CSRF disabled, filter registered, endpoints protected

Each has a failure mode that's easy to miss.

sections.title: JWT Validation Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    req["HTTP request with Authorization Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..."] --> filter["JwtAuthFilter (OncePerRequestFilter)"]
    filter --> hasHeader{"Header starts with Bearer?"}
    hasHeader -->|No| chainNext["chain.doFilter -> downstream filters handle anonymous"]
    hasHeader -->|Yes| parse["Parse JWT: split header.payload.signature, base64url-decode header and payload"]
    parse --> verify["Verify signature: HMAC-SHA256 with shared secret OR RSA-SHA256 with public key from JWKS"]
    verify --> sigOk{"Signature valid?"}
    sigOk -->|No| reject["SignatureException -> 401"]
    sigOk -->|Yes| claims["Check claims: exp not expired, nbf in past, iss matches expected, aud matches expected, alg matches expected"]
    claims --> claimsOk{"All claims valid?"}
    claimsOk -->|No| rejectClaims["ExpiredJwtException or InvalidClaimException -> 401"]
    claimsOk -->|Yes| authorities["Load authorities from roles claim, build SimpleGrantedAuthority list"]
    authorities --> setCtx["Build UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken (subject, null credentials, authorities), set in SecurityContextHolder"]
    setCtx --> chainNext2["chain.doFilter -> authorization check -> controller"]
```

sections.title: Token Generation: Claims, Algorithm, Expiry
sections.content:
**At login (after `AuthenticationManager` validates credentials):**

```java
public String generateToken(Authentication authentication) {
    Instant now = Instant.now();
    List<String> roles = authentication.getAuthorities().stream()
        .map(GrantedAuthority::getAuthority)
        .toList();

    return Jwts.builder()
        .subject(authentication.getName())
        .claim("roles", roles)
        .issuedAt(Date.from(now))
        .expiration(Date.from(now.plus(15, ChronoUnit.MINUTES)))
        .signWith(secretKey)
        .compact();
}
```

**Expiry strategy — 15-30 min for access tokens:**
- A stolen token is usable until expiry
- No way to invalidate a valid JWT without a blocklist
- Short expiry limits damage window
- Pair with a longer refresh token (hours/days, `HttpOnly` cookie, rotated)
- Refresh token can be DB-backed and validated on each use — refresh is infrequent so cost is acceptable

**Never put sensitive data in claims:**
- Payload is **base64URL-encoded, not encrypted**
- Anyone with the token can decode without the secret key
- Store only IDs and roles — never passwords, PII, or internal system IDs

**Signing algorithm choice:**
- **HS256** — one shared secret (simpler, single service)
- **RS256** — private key signs, public key verifies; public key distributable to all resource servers
- **ES256** — same as RS256 but smaller keys, faster
- For any microservice architecture: prefer RS256 or ES256 — eliminates secret distribution
- Publish public key at JWKS endpoint (`/.well-known/jwks.json`)

sections.title: The Authentication Filter (OncePerRequestFilter)
SecurityFilterChain: Three Settings That Must Be Right
sections.content:
**The configuration ties everything together:**

```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http,
                                               JwtAuthFilter jwtAuthFilter) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
        .sessionManagement(session -> session
            .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/auth/login", "/auth/register").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
        .build();
}
```

**`SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS`:**
- Prevents Spring Security from creating HTTP sessions
- Without it, every authenticated request creates a session object
- Session does nothing useful (JWT is stateless), but consumes memory
- 1000 req/sec server -> significant GC pressure

**`csrf.disable()` — safe here, dangerous if misapplied:**
- JWT in `Authorization` header can't be included in cross-site requests
- Browsers don't auto-attach headers (only cookies)
- If you later move JWT to `HttpOnly` cookie, **re-enable CSRF**

**`addFilterBefore` placement is critical:**
- JWT filter must run before `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`
- Populates `SecurityContext` before authorization decisions
- Register the filter as a `@Bean` — no `@Component` needed
- Spring Boot auto-registers all `Filter` beans -> would double-apply without exclusion via `FilterRegistrationBean.setEnabled(false)` or by not annotating with `@Component`

sections.title: JWT Custom Filter: Helps, Hurts, Watch For
sections.content:
**When it helps:**
- You ARE the token issuer (no external IdP)
- Need full control over claims, lifecycle, rotation
- Custom token validation logic beyond standard claims
- Single-service or trusted internal architecture

**When Resource Server is better:**
- You consume tokens issued elsewhere (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, Cognito)
- Standard OIDC/OAuth2 flows
- Need automatic JWKS key rotation handling
- Multi-tenant validation against multiple issuers

**When it hurts:**
- Re-implementing what `oauth2ResourceServer().jwt()` already does
- Storing tokens in `localStorage` -> XSS exposure
- Long-lived access tokens (24h+) without revocation -> huge blast radius
- Forgetting `STATELESS` -> phantom sessions, memory leak under load

**Watch for:**
- **Algorithm confusion** — pin allowed algorithms; reject `alg: none`
- **Clock skew** — `exp` rejects with seconds of drift; allow tolerance
- **`alg` from token header** — never trust it; configure expected algorithm in validator
- **Filter double-registration** — `FilterRegistrationBean` to disable Boot auto-registration
- **`SecurityContext` leakage** — set per request; cleared by `SecurityContextPersistenceFilter` automatically
- **Refresh tokens in localStorage** — even worse than access tokens; use `HttpOnly` cookie
- **Logout on client** doesn't actually invalidate the token — use a `jti` blocklist for real logout

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JWT filter must run before `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`** — `addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)`.
- **Store JWTs in `HttpOnly` cookies, not `localStorage`** — `HttpOnly` is JS-inaccessible, prevents XSS theft.
- **Short `exp` + refresh token rotation** — access 15min, refresh 7-30 days in `HttpOnly` cookie, rotate on use.
- **Verify `alg`, `iss`, `aud` claims** — `alg: none` has no signature; pin the expected algorithm; bind `iss`/`aud` to expected values.
- **Don't store user data in JWT** — payload is base64-visible; only `sub`, `iss`, `exp`, `iat`, and required claims; fetch sensitive data from a service.
- **`SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS`** prevents phantom sessions in JWT-only apps.
- **Prefer Spring's `oauth2ResourceServer().jwt()`** for standard OAuth2/OIDC validation — saves writing the filter.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The filter implementation**
- Extend `OncePerRequestFilter`
- Extract `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header
- Validate JWT: signature, `exp`, `alg`, `iss`, `aud`
- Build `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(sub, null, authorities)`
- `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth)`
- Register: `http.addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)`

**Token storage**
- `HttpOnly` cookie: JS-inaccessible, XSS-safe, needs CSRF protection if cookie-based
- `localStorage`: XSS-vulnerable, any script reads and exfiltrates
- For SPAs: short-lived access token in memory + long-lived refresh in `HttpOnly` cookie

**Refresh token rotation**
- Access token 15min TTL; client refreshes silently
- Refresh token 7 days; on use, issue new + revoke old
- Reuse of revoked refresh token signals theft -> revoke entire family

**SecurityFilterChain settings**
- `csrf.disable()` — safe with `Authorization` header
- `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS` — no phantom sessions
- `addFilterBefore` — JWT filter before UsernamePassword filter

**Best alternative for non-issuers**
- `spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server` + `oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))`
- `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://...`
- JWKS rotation handled automatically

**Common security mistakes**
- Catching JWT exceptions in filter -> security bypass
- Long-lived access tokens -> revocation impossible
- Trusting `alg` from token header -> algorithm confusion
- Putting PII in claims -> data exposure

questions.question: What are the security considerations for JWT — signing algorithms, expiry, and refresh token rotation?
questions.title: JWT Security — Signing, Expiry, and Refresh Token Rotation
questions.direct_answer: JWTs must be signed with a strong algorithm (**RS256/ES256** or HS256 with a secure key) to prevent forgery. **Access tokens should be short-lived (5-15 min)**; refresh tokens enable session continuity. **Refresh token rotation** — new refresh token per use, old one invalidated — provides automatic theft detection: reuse of an invalidated token signals compromise and the entire family is revoked. The biggest pitfalls: **algorithm confusion attack** (never trust `alg` from the token header — pin it), **`alg: none`** (always reject), **`localStorage` storage** (XSS-readable — use `HttpOnly` cookies), and **JWT `jti` blocklist in Redis** for explicit revocation/logout.

sections.title: JWT Security Has Multiple Layers, Each With a Known Attack
sections.content:
**Algorithm confusion** is the most subtle attack: some JWT libraries accept the algorithm from the token's own header without validation.
- An attacker takes a valid RS256 token, changes `alg` to `HS256`, and signs the modified payload with the server's **public** key (publicly available by definition).
- If the library uses the token-declared algorithm and treats the public key as the HS256 secret, the forged token validates.
- **Fix:** always enforce the expected algorithm server-side; never trust the `alg` header.

**`alg: none`** disables signature verification entirely. A token with `"alg": "none"` carries no signature — anyone can modify the payload. Modern libraries reject `none` by default; older versions and misconfig don't. Always pin the expected algorithm.

**Expiry management** is the second concern.
- JWTs cannot be revoked until they expire — the fundamental statelessness trade-off.
- A 24-hour access token = a 24-hour stolen-token window.
- **Short-lived access tokens (15-30 min)** + **longer-lived refresh tokens** (days, `HttpOnly` cookie) balance security and UX.

**Token storage determines XSS exposure.** `localStorage` is readable by any JS — one XSS = all tokens stolen. `HttpOnly` cookies are never JS-accessible; the browser attaches them automatically (which reintroduces CSRF risk, manageable with `SameSite=Lax` or CSRF tokens). For browser clients, **`HttpOnly` cookies are the stronger choice**.

sections.title: JWT Validation Pipeline
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    token["Incoming JWT in Authorization header"] --> parse["Parse: header.payload.signature, base64url-decode header and payload"]
    parse --> alg["Read alg from token header"]
    alg --> pinCheck{"alg matches expected pinned algorithm?"}
    pinCheck -->|No - prevents alg none and confusion| rej1["Reject: invalid algorithm"]
    pinCheck -->|Yes| sig["Verify signature: HMAC for HS256 with secret OR RSA verify for RS256 with public key from JWKS"]
    sig --> sigOk{"Signature valid?"}
    sigOk -->|No| rej2["Reject: signature mismatch"]
    sigOk -->|Yes| exp["Check exp claim against current time with small skew tolerance"]
    exp --> expOk{"Not expired?"}
    expOk -->|No| rej3["Reject: token expired"]
    expOk -->|Yes| nbf["Check nbf claim and iat claim are sane"]
    nbf --> issAud["Validate iss matches expected issuer and aud matches expected audience"]
    issAud --> jti["Check jti against revocation blocklist in Redis if logout or revocation supported"]
    jti --> blocked{"In blocklist?"}
    blocked -->|Yes| rej4["Reject: token revoked"]
    blocked -->|No| auth["Map roles claim to GrantedAuthority list, build Authentication, set SecurityContext"]
```

sections.title: HS256 vs RS256: Choosing the Signing Algorithm
sections.content:
The signing algorithm determines who can verify and how keys are managed.

| Aspect | HS256 (HMAC-SHA256) | RS256 (RSA-SHA256) |
|---|---|---|
| **Key type** | Symmetric — one secret signs and verifies | Asymmetric — private signs, public verifies |
| **Key sharing** | Every verifier needs the secret | Only auth server needs the private key |
| **Key compromise risk** | Single secret leak breaks everything | Private key stays on auth server; public is safe |
| **Performance** | Faster — HMAC hash | Slower — RSA crypto operation |
| **JWKS support** | Not standard | Yes — public key at `/.well-known/jwks.json` |
| **Multi-service** | Secret must be securely distributed | Public key shared freely; no risk |
| **Best for** | Single service, controlled environment | Microservices, OAuth2, public APIs |

**Why HS256 hurts in microservices:**
- Ten verifiers means ten places where the secret can leak
- Rotation requires coordinated update across all services
- Breach in any service compromises token issuance globally

**Why RS256 wins:**
- Private key stays on auth server
- Resource servers download public key from JWKS endpoint and cache it
- No secret to share, commit to Git, or rotate across services
- `kid` (key ID) in the JWT header lets validators pick the right key for seamless rotation

**ES256** (ECDSA) is the modern alternative — same security as RS256 with smaller keys (256-bit vs 2048-bit RSA) and faster operations.

sections.title: Refresh Token Rotation and JTI Blocklists
sections.content:
Two production patterns address JWT's revocation limitation.

**Refresh token rotation — automatic compromise detection:**
- Each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one
- Store refresh tokens in DB with `status` flag
- If attacker steals a refresh token and uses it first:
  - Server issues new token to attacker, invalidates old
  - Legitimate user's next refresh presents the now-invalid old token
  - Server detects reuse -> revoke entire family
  - User logged out; attacker's token stops working
- Proactive theft detection without an access-token blocklist

**JTI blocklist for logout/compromise:**
- `jti` (JWT ID) claim uniquely identifies each token
- Generate with `UUID.randomUUID().toString()` at issue
- On logout: store `jti` in Redis with TTL = remaining token validity
- On each request: check `jti` against Redis before accepting

**Why the blocklist stays small:**
- 15-minute access tokens -> blocklist entries live ≤15 min
- Redis TTL handles cleanup automatically
- 10K concurrent users + 15-min tokens = ≤10K Redis entries (trivial)

**`@Bean` example for the blocklist check:**

```java
@Component
public class JwtRevocationCheck {
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public boolean isRevoked(String jti) {
        return Boolean.TRUE.equals(redis.hasKey("revoked:" + jti));
    }

    public void revoke(String jti, Duration remaining) {
        redis.opsForValue().set("revoked:" + jti, "1", remaining);
    }
}
```

**Never store sensitive data in claims:**
- Payload is base64URL-encoded, not encrypted
- Any holder decodes with `atob()` in JS
- Store IDs, roles, non-sensitive metadata only
- PII, financial data, internal system IDs must never appear

sections.title: JWT Security: Helps, Hurts, Watch For
sections.content:
**When short expiry helps:**
- Limits damage of stolen access token to minutes
- Refresh rotation gives compromise detection
- Session control without abandoning statelessness

**When refresh rotation helps:**
- Detects token theft automatically
- No need for global access-token blocklist
- Industry standard (OAuth2 BCP)

**When JTI blocklist helps:**
- Explicit logout requirement (compliance)
- Forced revocation on account compromise
- Multi-device session management

**When it hurts:**
- Long-lived access tokens (hours+) without rotation -> revocation impossible
- HS256 secret in 10 microservices -> rotation nightmare
- Storing JWT in `localStorage` -> XSS-readable
- Trusting `alg` from token header -> algorithm confusion
- Embedding PII in claims -> data exposure on any leak

**Watch for:**
- **`alg: none`** — always reject
- **Algorithm confusion** — pin allowed algorithms in validator
- **Clock skew** — `exp` rejects with seconds of drift; allow small tolerance
- **Missing `aud` check** — token for service A accepted by service B
- **Long-lived JWT in mobile** — token theft via device compromise has huge window
- **`SameSite=Strict` + cookie JWT** — breaks SSO/payment redirects; use `Lax`
- **JWKS endpoint downtime** — cache public keys with stale-while-revalidate semantics

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HS256 (symmetric) vs RS256/ES256 (asymmetric)** — symmetric: shared secret; asymmetric: public verifier, private signer.
- **Algorithm confusion attack: never trust `alg` from the token header** — pin allowed algorithms in your validator config.
- **`alg: none`** disables signature verification — always reject explicitly.
- **Short expiry + refresh token rotation** prevents long-window compromise — access 15min, refresh 7-30 days, rotate on use.
- **JTI blocklist with Redis TTL** — `jti` of revoked tokens stored with TTL = remaining validity; one Redis check per request.
- **`nbf`/`iat` claims prevent replay** — validate `nbf` ≤ now ≤ `exp`; reject `iat` in the future.
- **Don't put PII in claims** — payload is base64-visible, not encrypted.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Signing algorithm choice**
- HS256 (HMAC): symmetric, same secret signs and verifies; all services need the secret; simpler for single service
- RS256 (RSA): asymmetric, auth server signs with private key, resource servers verify with public key from JWKS
- ES256 (ECDSA): asymmetric, smaller keys, faster than RSA; modern preferred

**Algorithm confusion attack**
- Attacker crafts token with `alg: none` -> no signature
- Vulnerable libraries derive algorithm from token header
- Fix: pin the expected algorithm in validator config

**Expiry strategy**
- Access token 15-min TTL — short exposure window
- Refresh token 7-30 days, `HttpOnly` cookie
- Rotation: each refresh issues new + revokes old; reuse of revoked = theft signal -> revoke family

**Revocation**
- Store revoked `jti` in Redis with TTL = remaining valid time
- Check on every request — one Redis lookup
- Enables instant logout and compromise response

**Storage rules**
- `HttpOnly` cookie -> XSS-safe; needs CSRF protection
- `localStorage` -> XSS-readable; never for tokens
- For SPAs: short access in memory + refresh in `HttpOnly` cookie

**Common mistakes**
- `alg: none` accepted by older libraries
- Algorithm confusion (RS256 -> HS256 with public key as secret)
- Long-lived access tokens (hours) without refresh
- PII in claims (base64 visible)
- HS256 secret leaked from one of many services

**Operational checklist**
- Pin algorithm; reject `alg: none`
- Validate `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, signature
- Use RS256/ES256 + JWKS for multi-service
- Refresh rotation for theft detection
- JTI blocklist for explicit revocation
